evidence: createApp only defines Express routes and calls OrderService methods (addProduct, placeOrder, getOrder, transitionOrder, cancelOrder).
Error middleware maps NotFoundError to 404, InsufficientStockError/DomainError to 409 and SyntaxError to 400. This is HTTP transport work.
objectBody/stringField/numberField/parseItems/parseState only check request shape and types; they contain no business rules.
The default parameter `new OrderService(new InMemoryFulfilmentStore())` is composition-root wiring, which is fine in infrastructure.
Minor smell: the input checks throw DomainError, so malformed requests get 409 instead of 400. This is error classification, not a business rule in the wrong layer.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/http-app.ts is an Express HTTP adapter, which is an infrastructure job. It defines routes and parses and checks the shape of requests (objectBody, stringField, numberField, parseItems, parseState). It also turns errors into HTTP status codes and wires a default OrderService with an InMemoryFulfilmentStore, as a composition root would. All of that belongs to infrastructure. Every business operation (addProduct, placeOrder, transitionOrder, cancelOrder, listOrders) is passed to the application service, and no stock, state-transition or pricing rules are implemented here. parseState only checks that the value is one of the allowed orderStates. That is input parsing, not a transition rule. One smell, which does not break this rule: the transport-level checks throw DomainError. Because the error handler maps DomainError to 409, malformed requests get 409 instead of 400. That is a problem with how errors are classified, not a business rule placed in the wrong layer.
